newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish construction groups posts strong earnings.
newsitem.headline: Swedish construction groups posts strong earnings.

text.p: Swedish construction groups Skanska and NCC posted a doubling of 1996 earnings on Tuesday and made shareholder-friendly moves, but warned of negative domestic construction market trends.

Skanska's 1996 profit after financial items leaped to 5.17 billion crowns ($698.5 million) from 2.57 billion, while NCC's surged to 462 million from 230 million. But Skanska's profit included a 1.76 billion capital gain on shares sold versus 25 million in 1995.
Still, Skanska's earnings were higher than expected with analysts in a Reuter poll targeting 4.93 billion crowns.
Both companies pointed, however, to weak Swedish construction market trends.

"According to the Swedish Construction Federation, construction activity will decrease by one percent in 1997," NCC said in a statement. "NCC's assessment of developments in the construction sector is more negative."

On the positive side, the companies continued to flirt with shareholders, Skanska by announcing a new dividend policy and planning a large capital transfer to shareholders and NCC by setting a price for NK Cityfastigheter of 55-64 crowns a share.

NCC said earlier in the month it would sell 60-75 percent of the department store and shopping mall properties company and list it on the Stockholm Stock Exchange. NCC has also made a public offer for Swedish rival Siab, which analysts favour.
"There is a trend towards streamlining and the moves cause ripples in the market," Stefan Sundblom, analyst at Swedbank, told Reuters.

Skanska's new dividend policy means a long-term intention to pay a dividend of 3-4 percent of adjusted equity and the company proposed to double 1996 dividends to 10 crowns a share from five, while analysts had expected 5.75 crowns.
"They increased the dividend much more than anyone had expected," said Sundblom.
Furthermore, the company said it planned to transfer 8-10 billion crowns in excess capital back to shareholders.
The money could be from a possible sale of Skanska's 25.9 percent stake in engineer Sandvik and its 8.7 percent holding in roller bearing company SKF, Sundblom said.

Skanska did not specify where the money would come from, but said: "Skanska has declared that its non-core business-related shareholdings constitute a financial reserve and that over time they will be divested."
Analysts approved of the new dividend policy saying it favoured shareholders but were sorry that Skanska, contrary to speculation, would not break up the company.
"If you think the share will keep advancing, a break up of the group is required," said Mikael Petersson at Aros Securities.
"Almost all conglomerates' shares are traded at a discount. Skanska is a conglomerate and is currently trading at a discount of 10-15 percent."
Skanska's share ended lower in disappointment at the no-break-up news, down two to 340, while NCC dropped 1.5 to 94 crowns, possibly hurt by its gloomy market view.
Analysts would have liked to see Skanska broken up into a building company, a construction company, an industry construction company and a holding company taking over Skanska's share portfolio.
